title: Sustainable Farming Practices
summary: This lesson explores organic methods, agroforestry, and climate‑friendly techniques that help protect the environment while keeping farms productive. Students will learn how these practices work together to create resilient agricultural systems.

sections.heading: Organic Farming Basics
sections.body:
Organic farming avoids synthetic chemicals and focuses on natural inputs such as compost, manure, and biological pest control. By building healthy soil, crops become more resistant to disease and need fewer external inputs.

Farmers use crop rotations, cover crops, and mulches to maintain soil fertility and suppress weeds. These practices also improve water retention, which is crucial during dry periods.

sections.heading: Agroforestry: Trees on the Farm
sections.body:
Agroforestry integrates trees and shrubs into agricultural fields, creating multiple layers of production. Trees provide shade, windbreaks, and habitats for beneficial insects, while also producing timber, fruit, or nuts.

The root systems of trees help prevent soil erosion and capture carbon from the atmosphere. Farmers can harvest tree products without harming the underlying crops, making the system both productive and sustainable.

sections.heading: Climate‑Friendly Techniques
sections.body:
Climate‑friendly farming reduces greenhouse‑gas emissions and adapts to changing weather patterns. Practices include reduced tillage, which lowers soil disturbance and keeps carbon stored underground.

Water‑saving methods such as drip irrigation and rainwater harvesting deliver moisture directly to plant roots, cutting waste. Combining these techniques with renewable energy (e.g., solar pumps) further lowers a farm's carbon footprint.

key_terms.meaning: A system that relies on natural inputs and excludes synthetic chemicals.
The intentional integration of trees and shrubs into agricultural landscapes.
A crop grown primarily to protect and improve soil rather than for harvest.
A soil management practice that minimizes plowing to preserve soil structure and carbon.
A water‑delivery system that releases small amounts of water directly to plant roots.

quiz.q: Which practice helps store carbon in the soil?
quiz.why: Reduced tillage disturbs the soil less, allowing more carbon to remain stored.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a cover crop?
options: To protect and improve soil health
quiz.why: Cover crops protect soil from erosion and add nutrients, enhancing soil health.

quiz.q: Which benefit does agroforestry provide to a farm?
options: Wind protection and habitat for beneficial insects
quiz.why: Trees act as windbreaks and create habitats for insects that help control pests.

quiz.q: Drip irrigation is most effective because it:
options: Delivers water directly to plant roots
quiz.why: Targeted delivery reduces water waste and supplies moisture where plants need it most.

flashcards.back: Farming that uses natural inputs and avoids synthetic chemicals.
Combining trees with crops or livestock to improve ecosystem services.
Minimizing soil disturbance to keep carbon stored and protect soil structure.
A crop grown to protect soil, add nutrients, and reduce erosion.
A system that delivers water directly to the root zone, conserving water.
